n: A widow of one of the prophets cries to Elisha: her faithful husband has died in debt, and the creditor is coming to take her two sons as slaves to work off what is owed. The law allowed debt servitude, but also called for compassion toward widows.

f.g: members of the prophetic communities Elisha led.

n: Elisha begins with what she already has. She has nothing but a small jar of oil. God often works with the little we bring Him.

f.g: female servant; a humble way of referring to herself.

n: He tells her to borrow as many empty jars as she can from her neighbors—“not a few.” The size of her blessing will match the size of her faith.
She is to shut the door and pour oil into every jar. The miracle happens privately, within the family.
She obeys, and her sons keep bringing jars as she pours.
When the last jar is full, the oil stops. The supply lasted exactly as long as there were vessels to receive it.
Elisha tells her to sell the oil, pay the debt, and live on the rest. The Lord provided not just rescue but a future.
In Shunem, a wealthy and influential woman insists that Elisha eat at her home, and he makes it a regular stop.

f.g: a village in the Jezreel Valley, on the route between Carmel and Samaria.
a woman of wealth and standing.

n: She recognizes Elisha as a holy man of God and proposes to her husband that they do more for him.
They build a small rooftop room furnished with a bed, table, chair, and lamp—a thoughtful act of hospitality to God’s servant.

f.g: a small upper room built on the roof.

n: On one visit Elisha rests in the room.
He sends his servant Gehazi to call the woman.

f.g: Elisha’s servant, appearing here for the first time.

n: Through Gehazi, Elisha offers to speak to the king or army commander on her behalf. She politely declines—she is content and secure among her own people.

f.w: careful for us with all this care
f.g: you have gone to so much trouble for us.

n: Gehazi notices what she lacks: she has no son, and her husband is old. In that society, a son meant both joy and future security.
Elisha calls her, and she stands respectfully in the doorway.
He promises that by this time next year she will hold a son. She begs him not to raise false hopes—her longing runs deep.

f.w: according to the time of life
f.g: when the season comes round again; about a year from now.

n: The promise is fulfilled; she bears a son at the time Elisha said.
Years later, the boy goes out to his father in the harvest fields.
He cries, “My head, my head!”—perhaps sunstroke. His father has a servant carry him home.
The boy sits on his mother’s lap until noon, then dies.
Without a word to anyone, she lays him on the prophet’s bed and shuts the door—an act of quiet faith that the man of God is the key.
She asks her husband for a servant and a donkey so she can hurry to Elisha.
Her husband, unaware of the death, wonders why she would go on an ordinary day. She simply says, “It will be well.”

f.g: holy days when people might visit a prophet.

n: She tells the servant to drive hard and not slow down for her sake.
She rides about twenty-five miles to Mount Carmel. Elisha sees her coming in the distance.
Elisha sends Gehazi to ask whether all is well. She answers, “It is well,” saving her grief for the prophet himself.

She falls and grasps Elisha’s feet in anguish. Gehazi tries to push her away, but Elisha stops him: she is in bitter distress, and the Lord has not revealed why. Prophets do not know everything unless God reveals it.

f.w: the LORD hath hid it from me

n: Her words reveal the tragedy: “Did I ask you for a son? Didn’t I tell you not to deceive me?”
Elisha sends Gehazi ahead with his staff, instructing him not to stop for greetings. Ancient greetings could be long and elaborate.

f.g: tuck your robe in your belt; get ready to move fast.

n: The mother refuses to leave without Elisha himself, using the same oath Elisha once spoke to Elijah. Elisha goes with her.
Gehazi lays the staff on the boy, but nothing happens. The child does not wake.
Elisha arrives to find the boy dead on his own bed.
He shuts the door and prays to the Lord. The power is God’s, not the prophet’s.
Elisha stretches himself over the child, mouth to mouth, eye to eye, hand to hand—just as Elijah once did—and the boy’s body grows warm.
After pacing and stretching himself out again, the boy sneezes seven times and opens his eyes. Seven suggests completeness: he is fully restored.
Elisha has Gehazi call the mother and tells her, “Take up your son.”
She falls at his feet in gratitude, then takes her son. Hebrews remembers such women: “Women received their dead raised to life again.”
During a famine at Gilgal, Elisha has a large pot of stew cooked for the prophets studying with him.
Someone gathers wild gourds from an unknown vine and slices them into the stew. Many think these were bitter, poisonous colocynth gourds.

f.g: probably colocynth, a bitter, poisonous gourd.

n: Tasting it, the men cry out, “There is death in the pot!”
Elisha throws in flour, and the stew becomes safe. As with the salt at Jericho, an ordinary substance becomes the means of God’s healing.
A man brings Elisha firstfruits—twenty barley loaves and fresh grain. Firstfruits were normally given to priests; here they go to God’s prophet.
Elisha’s servant protests that twenty loaves can’t feed a hundred men. Elisha says the Lord promises they will eat and have leftovers.
They eat and food is left over. This miracle foreshadows Jesus feeding the multitudes with barley loaves.
